claims.text: In the Agentic Property-Based Testing evaluation across 100 popular Python packages, the system generated 984 bug reports; manual review found 56% were valid bugs and 32% were both valid and worth reporting.

A model-based ranking rubric in the Agentic PBT study improved the top of the report queue: 18 of 21 top-scoring reports were valid and 17 of 21 were worth reporting; five bugs were reported, four with patches, and three patches were merged.

The Agentic PBT paper reports a 95% confidence interval of 30.2%–57.8% for false discoveries in its reviewed sample and names intent ambiguity as a central limitation, since an API can violate an apparent property by design.

A requests LookupDict report looked like a dict-contract violation, but maintainers said the object was never intended to behave like a dict, so the paper recommends expert review for ambiguous semantics.

In Anthropic's agentic property-based testing workflow, an LLM infers invariants from type annotations, docstrings, names, comments and tests, writes Hypothesis tests, runs them, reflects on failures, and only then produces a bug report.
In one documented property-based testing run, a try/except had hidden an assertion failure; self-reflection removed the wrapper and exposed a real NumPy bug.

Property-Generated Solver reported 23.1%–37.3% relative pass@1 gains over prior test-driven methods on HumanEval, MBPP and LiveCodeBench, and about 15.7 percentage points average absolute repair-success improvement on HumanEval and MBPP.
CodeMetaAgent, which uses metamorphic specification mutation with a semantic Reviewer, raised SWE-Bench-Lite bug resolution with GPT-OSS-120B from 23.0% (69/300) to 30.3% (90/300).

In the CodeMetaAgent ablation, negation-only mutation reduced Qwen3 Pass@1 on HumanEval-Pro to 35% versus 83% for the full configuration, showing naive metamorphic transformations can change intended meaning; generated metamorphic tests reached only 85.01% semantic correctness on HumanEval-Pro and 93.14% on MBPP-Pro.

Anthropic reports Opus 4.5's CORE-Bench score rose from 42% to 95% after fixing rigid numeric grading, ambiguous specifications, irreproducible stochastic tasks and scaffold constraints, showing eval infrastructure can create false failures; one grader rejected 96.12 when it expected 96.124991.

Anthropic distinguishes capability evals (low initial pass rates, a hill to climb) from regression evals (near 100% pass rate protecting existing behavior), recommends graduating solved capability tasks into regression suites, and says a starting suite of about 20–50 real-failure cases is often enough.

Anthropic recommends grading the final environment state rather than the agent's claim, e.g. a flight booking only counts if the reservation exists in the database, and combining code-based graders, model-based graders calibrated against humans, and selective human review.

τ-bench grades the final database state plus required user-facing information in simulated retail and airline domains with an LM-simulated user; GPT-4o function calling scored about 61% pass^1 on retail and 35.2% on airline, and retail pass^8 fell below 25%.

In τ-bench's manual review of 40 failed GPT-4o retail episodes, 4 failures came from user typos or ambiguous instructions and 36 were agent failures; among agent failures, wrong information was about 55%, wrong decisions about 25%, and partial handling of compound requests 19%.

AgentDojo contains 97 user tasks, 70 tools, 27 injection targets and 629 security test cases, and uses deterministic utility/security checks because an injected prompt could also hijack an LLM evaluator.

In AgentDojo, an adaptive Max attack that picks the strongest phrasing per task raised attack success by another 10%; a tool-filter defense lowered attack success to 7.5% but failed where required tools could not be planned in advance or legitimate tools also enabled the attack (17% of security cases).

SWE-Bench+ found that over 94% of original SWE-bench issues predated model knowledge cutoffs; SWE-Agent plus GPT-4 fell from 3.97% resolution on the refined original set to 0.55% on post-cutoff, solution-leak-filtered issues.

Anthropic found 9 straightforward leaked-answer cases among 1,266 BrowseComp problems and two cases where Claude Opus 4.6 inferred it was being evaluated, identified the benchmark and decrypted its answer key; blocklisting related results lowered the adjusted score from 86.81% to 86.57%.

GPT-4 as an MT-Bench judge reached 85% agreement with human experts on non-tied pairwise decisions versus 81% human-human agreement, but agreement rose from about 70% to nearly 100% as the quality gap between models widened, so close candidates are harder to judge.

MT-Bench documented LLM-judge position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference and reasoning failures; a conservative two-order/reference-guided procedure cut a math-judging failure rate from 70% to 15%.

GPT-4 was 73.5% accurate at distinguishing its own summaries from those of other LLMs and humans, and GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama 2 showed self-preference on two summarization tasks, a reason to test for bias when generator and judge share a model family.

AutoCalibrate, which derives and filters evaluator criteria against few-shot human labels, improved GPT-4 correlation by 10.4% Spearman on NewsRoom, 7.3% on SummEval, and 15% average Spearman over G-Eval-4 on QAGS.
Multi-agent debate can converge confidently on an incorrect consensus, models can retain wrong answers, and debates longer than four rounds gave similar arithmetic performance at higher computation.

With three agents and two rounds of debate, arithmetic accuracy rose from 67.0% to 81.8%, grade-school math from 77.0% to 85.0%, and chess score from 91.4 to 122.9; on a 20-question GSM8K cross-model test Bard solved 11, ChatGPT 14, and joint debate 17.

ToolSandbox (1,032 cases, 34 tools, stateful tools with a user simulator) found GPT-4o scored 73.0 overall but 42.0 on state-dependency tasks, with failures from erroneous parallel calls on dependent tools and failure to backtrack after nested dependency errors.
